- [FACT] The user is curious about meditation and spirituality.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Hinduism views God as an omnipotent and omnipresent being, with multiple gods and goddesses, and the ultimate goal is to achieve Moksha.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Sikhism views God as a formless and genderless entity, believing in one God, with the ultimate goal being union with God through meditation and living a truthful and ethical life.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] In Sikhism, meditation is known as Naam Simran, which means "remembering God through repetition of the divine name."
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The practice of Seva, or selfless service, is emphasized in Sikhism as a form of meditation.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Meditation in Sikhism is seen as a way to connect with the divine and develop a deeper spiritual understanding.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] A common posture for Sikh meditation is Sukhasana or Easy Pose, where the person sits cross-legged with hands resting on their knees.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The technique of Naam Simran involves continuously chanting the name of God, usually "Waheguru," to calm the mind and bring inner peace.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Some Sikhs use meditation beads called Mala for Naam Simran, repeating the name of God with each bead.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Sikhs typically practice meditation during the early morning hours, around 3am, known as Amrit Vela or the "Ambrosial Hours."
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The Amrit Vela is considered an auspicious time for meditation, believed to deepen one's connection with God.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Sikhs can meditate at any time of the day, but early morning is considered most effective due to a fresh mind.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Some Sikhs also practice meditation before bedtime to calm the mind and promote restful sleep, and before eating food to express gratitude to God.
